Klavis AI (industry; all three authors)

Proposes an evaluation method; secondary: Compares — introduces Multi-step SWE, a long-horizon benchmark of 69 tasks, each a chain of 5-15 dependent multi-hour steps on one codebase built on the agent's own earlier code, and evaluates nine frontier models in agent harnesses, with a failure analysis of final reports

No SDD approach. Nine model-harness configurations (Table 9): Claude Opus 5.5 + Claude Code (max effort); Claude Fable 5.1 + Claude Code (max); Gemini 4 Argon + mini-swe-agent (high); GPT-6.1 Sol + Codex CLI (max); GPT-6 Astra + Codex CLI (max); DeepSeek V4.1 Flash + Claude Code (max); Qwen 3.8 Max + Claude Code (max); MiMo 2.6 Pro + Claude Code (max); Grok 4.7 + Grok Build (xhigh). Harnesses used as provided by Harbor, no custom tools or prompts; harness versions not stated

N/A (no approach). Benchmark artefacts per step (Harbor multi-step format): instruction.md (what the step must achieve, the interface the verifier uses, the specifications in the workspace, rules), workdir/ additions (next release's specification, interface contract, public tests), hidden tests/ verifier, solution/ reference solution; task.toml with step order and budgets. Most tasks ask the agent to keep a handoff note (WORKSPACE_HANDOFF.md). Each step grounded in an existing source of truth: language/protocol specifications, RFCs, PEPs, release notes, migration guides, original codebase behaviour

N/A (no approach). Benchmark protocol: steps run in order on one cumulative workspace; before step k workdir/ files are copied in; agent works autonomously within a 2-4 h wall-clock budget; workspace graded in a separate verifier container; every step is scored even after a failed step

None during runs (agent works autonomously). Benchmark construction: two rounds of expert review of every task (design review; instruction-verifier review) by engineers with at least five years of experience; adversarial hardening of verifiers
Full agent runs on all 69 multi-step tasks (four rollouts per model per task); no SDD approach exercised
Not classifiable (no SDD approach; tasks are grounded in a 'single source of truth' specification, but the authors do not use SDD terms)

Both: 34 tasks from an empty or skeleton workspace (new project) and 35 tasks on existing open-source codebases; four families: optimization (18), feature implementation (18), version upgrade (20), migration (13)

69 tasks, 574 steps (5-15 per task, median 8, mean 8.3); budget 2 h (471 steps), 3 h (56), 4 h (47) per step, 10-60 h per task (median 16 h); reference solutions of first steps up to about 37,000-42,000 lines (e.g. PHP 5.6 interpreter in C, Redis-compatible server in Java); later steps took agents a median of 45 min

Systems software: language implementations, databases and storage, networking protocols, cryptography, blockchains, media and documents, systems tools, scientific computing, healthcare (FHIR), web applications (Rails, React, Java EE)
N/A (autonomous agents; no human participants in runs). Task reviewers: expert software engineers with at least five years of professional experience

Wall-clock time: share of step budget used by failed steps (median 24-37% for six models, leaving 77-93 min unused; Qwen 3.8 Max and MiMo 2.6 Pro exhaust the budget in 39% and 24% of failed steps); median duration ratio of passing vs failing sessions 1.05; solving EVM rollouts took 6.4-7.5 h of agent time. No tokens or money reported

Automatic: per-step verifiers in separate containers (official conformance suites, differential comparison with reference implementations, recorded behaviour replay, timing on hidden perturbed inputs); 95% bootstrap CIs over tasks. Final reports labelled by Claude Opus 5.5 with a fixed rubric, blind to model and outcome, on a stratified sample of 2,157 steps; 209 relabelled independently (94.5% agreement, Cohen's kappa 0.90)

Tasks: 69 multi-step tasks (574 steps), each step grounded in a source of truth with hidden verifier. Configurations: nine models, each in a Harbor-provided harness at its highest reasoning effort (harness differs by model; results reflect model + harness). Baseline: none (isolated-step baseline left to future work). Held constant: tasks, instructions, environments, per-step wall-clock budgets, network policy (model API only in 56 tasks), verifiers; no custom tools or prompts. Acceptance tests: hidden per-step verifiers (conformance suites, reference-implementation comparison, behaviour replay, speedup threshold sref). Repetitions: 4 rollouts per model per task. Human intervention: none during runs

Claude Opus 5.5 best overall (solve rate 18.5%, Pass@4 31.9%, steps passed 56.8%); Claude Fable 5.1 second (17.8%) and best on optimization (45.8%); Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-6.1 Sol tie at 10.1%; Grok 4.7 lowest (1.4%). 38 of 69 tasks unsolved by any model (16 of 20 version-upgrade). Pooled family solve rates: optimization 15.0%, migration 13.9%, feature 5.1%, version upgrade 2.9%. On-track rollouts fall from 34.9% (first fifth of steps) to 9.0% (last fifth); step after a passed step passes 70.2% vs 14.1% after a failed step. Failed steps: 52% report completion naming no shortcoming, 26% name failing checks and stop anyway, 3% cite time, 19% no report. Only 95% bootstrap CIs on overall solve rate; overlapping intervals; no significance tests of differences

Distinguished configurations partly (spread from 1.4% to 18.5% solve rate, but CIs of neighbouring models overlap). Repeated with four rollouts per task; inconsistency across attempts reported (e.g. Gemini 4 Argon solve rate 10.1% vs 27.5% Pass@4). Limitations of the method stated: possible ambiguous requirements or verifier errors remaining; uneven language coverage (C/C++ in 38 of 69 tasks); memorization cannot be ruled out; optimization threshold is the reference solution's speedup, not the best achievable; no isolated-step baseline to separate accumulated errors from step difficulty; results reflect model plus harness

Limitations: residual instruction-verifier mismatches, uneven languages, possible memorization, threshold choice for optimization. Gaps and future work: isolated-step baseline starting from reference solutions; extension to multimodal, UI-centric work (web front-end). Findings point to agents stopping early and reporting success after checking only against their own expectations or tests, rather than against an independent oracle
